subject: research/runlength-twin
professional: a senior statistician in simulation output analysis / MCMC diagnostics (fixed-width run-length rules, batch means, integrated autocorrelation time) who also validates controllers for hardware test campaigns; first checks: is the variance of the time-averaged cost right for an autocorrelated loop, do the run lengths and coverages reproduce, and is the twin-sized procedure being criticised one a practitioner would actually use instead of estimating the variance from the real run

evidence.correctness: Every headline number reproduces from an independent script that does not import the subject (/tmp/claude-0/audit-runlength-twin/recompute.py, numpy, /usr/bin/python3.13 -I): scalar DARE solved in closed form (positive root of b^2P^2+(r-qb^2-a^2r)P-qr=0) instead of the subject's fixed-point iteration, relative variance from the textbook double sum (2/n^2)[n+2 sum (n-k) rho^k] instead of the closed form, minimal n by linear scan. All 9 stable E2 cells checked match to the step: e.g. m=2,r=0.1 K=1.672, ac_real -0.772, ac_twin 0.128, n_twin 3177, n_real 12110, ratio 3.81, normal-approx coverage 0.685; m=0.5,r=5 4007/15069, 0.688; m=1.5,r=5 6837/3248, 0.996; m=3 unstable for r=0.1/1/5 (ac_real -1.649/-1.480/-1.441). A 20,000-run vectorised Monte Carlo gives real coverage 0.6851+-0.0064, 0.6930+-0.0064, 0.9949+-0.0010, so the normal approximation is accurate and the subject's 2,000-run 0.678/0.673 differ only by sampling noise. Independent pilot simulation (/tmp/claude-0/audit-runlength-twin/pilot.py, 5,000 reps) reproduces E6: medians 5084/5131/5141 vs 5142/5121/5123, P(n_hat<n_real) 0.53/0.51/0.51 vs 0.50/0.51/0.53, P(<0.8 n) 0.096/0.005/0.000 vs 0.11/0.01/0.00. The variance law itself (cov(x_t^2,x_{t+k}^2)=2 sigma^4 a_c^{2k} for Gaussian AR(1), Isserlis) is standard and correctly applied.
evidence.completeness: All claimed artefacts run end to end in a scratch copy: README 'unittest ... 11 tests, ~2 s' -> Ran 11 tests in 1.892s OK; experiments/run.py regenerates results.txt byte-identically (35 s here vs the README's '~15 s'); experiments/figure.py regenerates run_ratio.svg byte-identically; the served page https://marisstella.app/research/runlength-twin/ loads (HTTP 200) and states the same numbers. Next steps are listed as not done. No stubs or TODOs.
evidence.verification: `PYTHONPATH=src /usr/bin/python3.13 -m unittest discover -s tests`: 11 passed. Good: the closed form is tested against the double sum at 16 (n, rho) points and against simulation, and n_exact minimality is tested. Weak: five mutants via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py, four survived: halving the Riccati update term (model.py:20; the test only asserts 0<K<0.9), replacing the headline sizing ratio by (1-rho_t)/(1-rho_r) (model.py:85; tests only check =1 at equal rho and the sign of the inequality), squaring the coverage scale (model.py:80; same inequality-only tests), and the pilot clip 0.999->0.9 (model.py:111). Only the rel_var exponent mutant (model.py:43) was caught. The two formulas that carry the paper's headline (sizing ratio, coverage) and the LQR gain have no pinned-value test.
evidence.craft: Read src/runlength_twin/model.py, experiments/run.py, experiments/figure.py, tests/test_model.py. 115-line stdlib module, clear docstring deriving the formula, rel_var validates rho. Defects: riccati_gain returns silently after 100,000 iterations without signalling non-convergence; pilot_rho divides by zero on a constant pilot and clips rho at 0.999 silently; experiments/run.py E5 re-implements the simulate_rel_var loop instead of reusing it; `from .model import *` package API; pure-Python Monte Carlo makes the run 35 s where numpy would be under 5 s (a stated design choice: no dependencies).
evidence.claims: Every README and paper number traced to experiments/results.txt and reproduced (3,177 vs 12,110; 4,007 vs 15,069; 2.1x; 0.685/0.688, simulated 0.678/0.673; 5,142 vs 5,145; unstable m=3). Limitations, 'Preliminary', non-affiliation and MIT stated; references are real (Geyer 1992 Stat Sci 7(4); Glynn & Whitt 1992 Oper Res 40(3); Anderson 1971). Small misstatements: the figure labels m as 'gain multiplier' (it multiplies the twin's plant pole) and r as 'noise ratio' (it is the LQR control weight), and its aria-label says the ratio is one only at m=1 although the r=1 curve crosses 1 between m=1.5 (0.71) and m=2 (1.22); the paper title rounds 3.8x to '4x'; 'E1-E4 are exact formulas' while E4's coverage is a normal approximation; README:13 asserts that the named CU Boulder labs budget hardware run length from simulated rollouts with no citation.
evidence.fitness: A researcher can rerun and extend it in minutes, and the exact finite-n variance plus the observation that a negative closed-loop pole averages x^2 as slowly as a positive one are correct and usable. But the result is the classical integrated autocorrelation time (1+rho)/(1-rho) of an AR(1) (Geyer 1992; Sokal's IAT; Glynn & Whitt) applied to a ratio of two poles; nothing new in the statistics. Nearest prior work is fixed-width output analysis and sequential stopping rules (Glynn & Whitt 1992, Ann. Appl. Prob. 2(1); Jones, Haran, Caffo & Neath 2006, JASA; Flegal & Jones 2010, Ann. Stat.; Vats, Flegal & Jones 2019 multivariate ESS), which estimate the variance from the real run itself with batch means or spectral estimators; the paper neither cites nor compares against them and lists sequential stopping only as a next step. The 0.685 coverage headline therefore describes a team that reports the twin's width without looking at its own data, a procedure a practitioner would not use. Not near the PhD/publishable bar in research/CLAUDE.md on its own; not linked into any programme in research/PROGRAMMES.md.
evidence.domain: The math matches the standard (Isserlis fourth moments, Bartlett-type variance of a correlated mean, scalar DARE). A senior output-analysis statistician would depart on the procedure: (a) the baseline should be the data-driven fixed-width rule (batch means / overlapping batch means / spectral IAT on the cost series, with a sequential stopping rule), against which the twin's role is only an initial run-length guess; (b) the pilot repair is a parametric AR(1) plug-in on x that requires the state to be observed and the model to be right, where practice estimates the IAT of the observed cost series model-free; the paper admits it is not a valid confidence procedure. Stated limits (scalar, Gaussian, stationary, known gain) are appropriate.

defects.what: No baseline against the standard data-driven procedure: fixed-width sequential stopping with batch-means or spectral variance estimated from the real run (Glynn & Whitt 1992 AAP; Jones et al. 2006; Flegal & Jones 2010) is neither cited nor compared, so the 0.685-coverage headline describes reporting the twin's width without looking at the run's own data, which a practitioner would not do; the core law is the textbook AR(1) integrated autocorrelation time, so novelty is overstated by omission

The formulas that carry the headline have no pinned-value tests: replacing sizing_ratio by (1-rho_t)/(1-rho_r), squaring the coverage scale, or halving the Riccati update all leave 11/11 tests green (4 of 5 mutants survived)

Figure mislabels m as 'gain multiplier' (it scales the twin's plant pole) and r as 'noise ratio' (it is the LQR control weight); aria-label says the ratio is one only at m=1 although the r=1 curve crosses 1 between m=1.5 and m=2
Paper says 'E1-E4 are exact formulas' though E4's coverage is a normal approximation, and the title rounds the measured 3.81x/3.76x up to '4x'

verdict: Correct and reproducible: every E2 cell, the coverages, the unstable m=3 cells and the pilot statistics reproduce from an independent numpy script using a closed-form DARE and the textbook double-sum variance, and a 20,000-run simulation confirms the normal-approximation coverage (0.6851 vs 0.685). It does not meet the bar because verification is weak (4 of 5 seeded bugs survive; the sizing-ratio and coverage formulas behind the headline are untested by value) and because, as research, it is the classical AR(1) integrated-autocorrelation-time result applied to two poles, compared against a strawman (reporting the twin's width) rather than the standard fixed-width sequential stopping rule with batch-means variance from the real run. Small labelling slips in the figure and paper.
